PeakLogic is a multi-tenant, cloud-native IoT SaaS platform that monitors industrial and commercial equipment — pumping stations, HVAC systems, pool equipment, and QSR (quick-service restaurant) assets — in real time. title: Multi-Tenancy Model
text: PeakLogic uses a hybrid pooled model: all tenants share a single PostgreSQL database, but every tenant-scoped table carries a tenant_id column and PostgreSQL Row-Level Security (RLS) policies enforce data isolation at the database level. No application query can accidentally cross tenant boundaries because the database engine enforces it. v1.1.0 — RLS is now actually enforced against the app's own DB role Prior to v1.1.0, the application connected to PostgreSQL as peaklogic_admin — the same role that owns every table. PostgreSQL table owners silently bypass RLS by default unless FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY is explicitly set, which no table in this schema ever had. This meant every "RLS enforces isolation" claim in this platform's history, back to the very first migration, described a mechanism that would not have actually worked once deployed. text: described a mechanism that would not have actually worked once deployed. It was never live-exploited (nothing had been deployed to a real AWS account before this was found), but it is the single most important fact in this release. See §6.3 for full detail. Channel-partner access is a second, deliberately different scoping dimension layered on top of the tenant model above: a channel-partner session can read across every tenant attributed to it (via tenants.channel_partner_id ), and a technician's session is further restricted to the sites within their own assigned territory. text: This platform has never been deployed to a real AWS environment As of v1.1.0, no AWS account has ever been used with this project (confirmed directly with engineering leadership). Everything below is a reviewed, typechecked, tested-in-isolation procedure — not a proven runbook. Follow it carefully and expect to debug real first-deploy issues that can't be caught without a real account: a few are already known in advance and listed inline below. title: 6.3 Row-Level Security (RLS) — including the FORCE RLS fix
text: Read this box before touching RLS on this platform The v1.0.0 version of this guide said "as the peaklogic_admin superuser, RLS is bypassed automatically" — that framing was wrong, and describes exactly the bug this release fixed. peaklogic_admin is not a real PostgreSQL superuser (RDS never grants that on the master user) — it appeared to bypass RLS for a completely different reason: it owns every table (it's also the role every migration runs as), and PostgreSQL table owners silently bypass RLS by default, independent of superuser status, unless FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY is explicitly set on the table. title: 9. Alert Rules

To modify thresholds you must edit the source code and redeploy the Lambda. v1.1.0 — telemetry values are now validated before use A new sanitizeMetrics() function drops any metric value that isn't a finite number (null, a non-numeric string, NaN , Infinity ) before it reaches either the database INSERT or rule evaluation. title: Pump Rules

title: Refrigeration Rules (previously undocumented)
text: Measures the product temperature (a probe in the food/drink itself), not ambient air — this is deliberate: it lets the unit run warmer (saving energy) while still catching an actual food-safety violation early, the platform's dual energy/compliance pitch for this vertical. title: Alert Deduplication
text: Before creating a new alert, the ingest handler checks whether an open or acknowledged alert already exists for the same device, metric, and severity. If one exists, the ingest completes silently without creating a duplicate. This prevents alert storms during sustained threshold violations.

title: Auto-Ticket for Critical Alerts
text: When a CRITICAL alert is created, the ingest handler automatically: Looks up the tenant's settings.webhook_url from the tenants table Creates a service ticket with priority = emergency linked to the alert POSTs the ticket payload to the webhook URL via backend/shared/webhook.ts 's postWebhook() (fire-and-forget, 8-second timeout) v1.1.0 — Critical SSRF fix, live and exploitable in v1.0.0 POST /v1/tickets previously accepted an arbitrary webhookUrl directly from the request body with zero validation — any authenticated operator + user could make this Lambda send an outbound request anywhere they chose, including internal network reconnaissance. The same unguarded pattern existed a second time in this exact auto-webhook code path. Fixed with a shared, tested postWebhook() function: HTTPS-only, resolves the hostname, and rejects private/loopback/link-local address ranges (including 169.254.

title: Auto-Ticket for Critical Alerts
text: function: HTTPS-only, resolves the hostname, and rejects private/loopback/link-local address ranges (including 169.254.0.0/16 , which covers EC2's IMDS, ECS/Fargate's task-metadata endpoint, and Lambda's own AZ-metadata endpoint). title: Authentication Flow
text: The frontend uses AWS Amplify v6 with the tenant Cognito User Pool (§2.3) configured in frontend/src/amplify-config.ts . title: Backing Up Device Certificates
text: Device private keys cannot be re-downloaded from AWS after initial provisioning. Ensure the device-certs/ directory is backed up securely (encrypted storage, not git): # Create an encrypted zip of all device certificates # Store this in a secure, access-controlled location (not git) Compress-Archive -Path "device-certs" -DestinationPath "device-certs-backup-$(Get-Date -Format 'yyyyMMdd').zip" Note on Device Certificate Loss If a private key backup is lost, you must revoke the affected certificate(s) in IoT Core and re-provision the devices. The physical hardware will need to be reflashed with the new certificates. This is why secure off-git backup of device-certs is critical.

It's a website that watches your equipment for you — pumps, coolers, pool systems, and more — using small sensors. Instead of someone walking around checking things by hand, the sensors send readings automatically, and PeakLogic tells you the moment something looks wrong. It's growing into a bigger operations platform — with live equipment screens, on-site hubs that keep working even if the internet drops, automatic work orders, and compliance reports — but the day-to-day app in this guide works exactly as described. title: 2.3 Setting Up Your Second Login Step
text: PeakLogic requires a second login step beyond just your password — a fresh 6-digit code every time you sign in, generated by an app on your phone. This is standard practice for protecting business data and only needs to be set up once. Open the authenticator app on your phone (Google Authenticator or Microsoft Authenticator both work — install one free from your phone's app store if you don't have one yet). On your computer screen, you'll see a small square barcode-like image called a QR code . In your phone's authenticator app, tap the button to add a new account (usually a + icon), then choose "Scan a QR code." Point your phone's camera at the QR code on your screen — the app will automatically add "PeakLogic" to your list. Your phone will now show a 6-digit number that changes every 30 seconds. PeakLogic — User Guide · v1.3 · 2026-07-25 Written in plain language for everyone, technical or not.

title: About Fleet Overview
text: This is every site you manage, in one view. Green means healthy, amber means worth a look, red means it needs attention now. The top tiles summarize the whole estate; the "needs attention" list is sorted worst-first. Click any organization to open it in its own scoped view.

title: About this operator screen
text: Your live plant view. Each tile is a current reading from the equipment; the color is its state (green fine, amber off-setpoint, red critical). The alarm panel lists what needs attention, and the historian shows recent trends. This screen keeps working even if the internet drops — the on-site Hub serves it locally.

title: About PeakLogic Hubs
text: The small box installed at each site. A Hub reads your equipment and PLCs, watches for alarms locally, shows the operator screen on-site even without internet, and forwards data to the cloud. Green means online and syncing, amber means it is being set up, red means it is offline.

title: About Work Orders & PM
text: Maintenance work in one place. A critical or anomaly alarm automatically creates a work order and sends it to the servicing partner; preventive-maintenance (PM) schedules create work orders when they come due. Each work order moves through dispatched → accepted → on-site → completed.

title: About Compliance (DMR)
text: Automatic regulatory reporting. PeakLogic compiles the period’s monitored values into a regulator-ready draft (a Discharge Monitoring Report for wastewater). Review each parameter against its permit limit, then file it through your normal channel. You remain the filer of record — PeakLogic does not file for you.

title: Threshold alarm
text: A reading crossed a configured limit (for example, a level above its setpoint). What to check: compare the value to its normal range and the recent trend on this asset. If it is a real process change, acknowledge it and address the cause; if it looks like a bad reading, check the sensor.

title: AI anomaly alarm
text: A reading deviated from this asset’s own learned normal behavior — not a fixed limit. It is capped at "warning" and is not a confirmed fault on its own. What to check: look at the asset and the trend behind the value; a rising motor current, for example, can hint at wear. Create a work order if it warrants a look.

title: Device silent alarm
text: A device stopped sending readings when one was expected — different from a bad reading. It may be offline, disconnected, or failed. What to check: confirm the device has power and its Hub is online (see PeakLogic Hubs). It clears itself once the device reports again.

title: Acknowledge an alarm
text: 1) Find the alarm in the alarm panel. 2) Read its insight line (threshold, or an AI anomaly score). 3) Click Acknowledged to mark it seen so your team knows someone is on it. 4) If it needs a visit, create a work order from it — that dispatches a technician.

title: Read a trend in the historian
text: 1) Open the historian panel. 2) Pick the metrics you want to overlay (for example dissolved oxygen and flow). 3) Choose a range — last 24 hours, 7 days, 30 days, or custom. 4) Watch where lines diverge; that is usually where a problem starts. Export to CSV if you need it for a record.

title: Generate due preventive-maintenance work orders
text: 1) On Work Orders, click "Generate due PM work orders". 2) Every PM schedule that has reached its due date creates a work order. 3) Assign each to a technician if it is not already. Overdue schedules generate one work order for the next occurrence, not a backlog.

title: Generate a DMR draft
text: 1) On Compliance, confirm the reporting period. 2) Click "Generate DMR draft". 3) Review each parameter against its permit limit — exceedances and coverage gaps are flagged, never hidden or filled in. 4) File the reviewed report through your normal regulator channel.

title: No live data on a screen
text: First check the site’s Hub is online (PeakLogic Hubs). If the Hub is offline, the site still runs locally but cloud updates pause. If a single tile is frozen, that device may be silent — a "device silent" alarm will confirm it. If everything is blank, reload the screen.

title: A Hub shows offline
text: The site keeps operating on the Hub’s local copy of the operator screen; only cloud sync is paused. Check site connectivity (network/power at the Hub), not the plant equipment. Once the Hub reconnects, it forwards the data it buffered while offline and catches up automatically.

title: Operator daily rounds
text: Start on the operator screen: scan the tiles for anything amber or red. Clear the alarm panel — acknowledge what you have seen, create work orders for what needs a visit. Glance at the historian for anything trending the wrong way. Note anything for the next shift.

title: Monthly compliance filing
text: Near period end, open Compliance and generate the DMR draft. Review every parameter against its permit limit; investigate and document any exceedance, and note any coverage gap. When satisfied, file through your regulator channel. The immutable audit trail backs the numbers you filed.

title: Dissolved Oxygen (DO)
text: How much oxygen is dissolved in the water (mg/L). In an aeration basin it needs to stay above the setpoint: too little starves the biology, too much wastes blower energy.

title: ORP
text: Oxidation-reduction potential (mV) — a measure used in the anoxic zone to confirm the right reactions (like denitrification) are happening where they should.

title: RAS (Return Activated Sludge)
text: Sludge pumped from the clarifier back to the front of the process to keep the biology recirculating. If the RAS pump stops, the process backs up.

title: DMR (Discharge Monitoring Report)
text: A Discharge Monitoring Report — the periodic report a permitted wastewater facility files with the regulator, summarizing monitored values against permit limits.

title: PeakLogic Hub
text: The on-site box that reads your equipment and PLCs, evaluates alarms locally, serves the operator screen and this help offline, and forwards data to the cloud.

title: Tag
text: A named point that maps a raw source (a PLC register or a device metric) to a standard reading shown on your screens — so everything speaks one vocabulary regardless of the underlying device.
